analysis.one_liner: Restructures the labor board to require partisan balance and lets employers challenge union complaints in court early.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was introduced in June 2023 with zero cosponsors and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, without a single vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rework the National Labor Relations Board, the agency that enforces workers' rights to organize and unionize. It would expand the board from five to six members split evenly between the two parties, require the President to consult the opposing party's Senate leader before nominating members, and allow employers hit with a labor complaint to ask a federal court to shut down the case if the agency's top lawyer lacks substantial evidence. It would also force the board to finish cases within a year or lose control of them, and let courts review those decisions fresh, with no deference to the agency.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, especially those contesting union organizing drives or accused of firing workers for union activity. They could challenge complaints in court before any hearing, obtain the agency's internal legal memos, get any case final within a year on the agency's terms, and have judges review board decisions from scratch, with no deference to the agency's labor-law expertise. The even partisan split on the board would also make it harder for any administration to issue union-friendly rulings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers contesting union organizing and labor complaints

how_it_helps.text: Expands the board from five to six members split three-and-three between the two major parties, and requires a quorum to consist of equal numbers from each party, so neither party's appointees can control rulings alone [S2].
Requires the President to consult the Senate leader of the opposing party before nominating board members [S2].

Lets any person or company subject to a General Counsel complaint petition a federal district court within 30 days, and the court can block all further proceedings if it finds no substantial evidence of a violation [S2].
Requires the General Counsel to hand over internal advice memoranda and other agency memos related to a complaint within 10 days of a party's request [S2].

Requires the board to issue a final decision within one year of an administrative law judge's report or a regional director's decision; otherwise any party can have the case deemed final at that stage, and courts would review the agency's orders de novo, meaning with no deference to the board [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Workers who rely on the National Labor Relations Board to enforce their rights to organize, join a union, and bargain collectively. Early court challenges, discovery of the agency's internal strategy memos, mandatory partisan balance, and one-year deadlines would slow or weaken enforcement against employers who violate labor law, and union-side rulings would be easier to overturn in court.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers using the labor board to enforce organizing rights

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith case for the bill is that a five-member board can be captured by a single party's appointees, flipping workers' rights every time the White House changes hands, and that requiring the President to consult the opposing party's Senate leader could produce more moderate, durable appointments [S2].

Even an honest supporter would acknowledge the costs: a three-three board invites deadlock on contested cases, letting employers accused of illegal union-busting face no decision at all, and courts reviewing complaints early and agency orders de novo would substitute generalist judges for the specialized labor tribunal Congress created for these disputes [S2].

Revealing the General Counsel's internal advice memoranda to accused parties would expose the enforcement agency's legal strategy before any hearing, an advantage that runs one way, toward respondents, in a process where the board's general counsel acts as prosecutor [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill has a legitimate premise, that labor-board appointments have become thoroughly partisan and cases can drag on for years, but its remedies cut overwhelmingly in one direction. A court veto over complaints before any hearing, forced disclosure of the prosecutor's internal memos, and fresh judicial review of final orders would primarily benefit employers facing enforcement, while the mandated partisan split would more often produce deadlock than balance. The one-year deadline is the one provision that helps both sides. On the whole, the design burdens workers' enforcement machinery far more than it improves the process.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Walberg introduced the bill on June 5, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S4].
No cosponsors signed on at any point [S3].
The committee took no further action of any kind: no markup, no report, no floor vote, and the bill died at the end of the Congress [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the existing five-member labor board and its current enforcement process continue unchanged, so workers' organizing rights are enforced under the pre-existing rules rather than the weaker process this bill would have created. No group gained from the bill itself; its death simply preserved the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers, by default, since the enforcement status quo held

for.name: Rep. Tim Walberg
for.role: U.S. Representative, MI-5; sponsor of the bill
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Labor Relations Board Reform Act on June 5, 2023

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and never reached a vote, so no measurable partisan split ever formed.

industries.industry: Employers facing labor-board enforcement (especially in organizing and union-busting disputes)
industries.note: The bill would have given accused employers an early court veto over complaints, access to the agency's internal memos, and fresh judicial review of final orders. The industries facing the most board actions, retail, logistics, hospitality, and other low-wage sectors where union drives are concentrated, would have gained the most leverage against their own workers' organizing rights.

industries.industry: Labor unions and the union organizing ecosystem
industries.note: A three-three board, early judicial challenges, and de novo court review would have made union-friendly rulings harder to obtain and easier to overturn. Unions' interest here runs alongside the workers they organize.
